parts.title: Part I – Multiple Choice Questions
parts.instructions: Part I contains 60 questions. You must answer all of them. Each question carries 1.30 points. There is only one best answer for each question; blacken the letter of your choice on the Scantron answer sheet with a pencil.

parts.title: Part II – Completion and Short Answer Questions
parts.instructions: Part II contains thirteen completion and short answer questions. You must answer all of them. This part carries twenty two points. Write your answers on the separate answer sheet provided.

questions.stem: The eight levels of classification, from general to specific, are

options.A: kingdom, class, order, phylum, family, genus, species.
options.B: species, phylum, class, family, order, genus, kingdom.
options.C: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
options.D: kingdom, class, phylum, order, family, genus, species.
options.E: species, class, family, order, genus, phylum, kingdom.

explanation_steps: From the most general to the most specific the ranks are: kingdom → phylum → class → order → family → genus → species.
B and E run the wrong way and are scrambled; A and D put phylum in the wrong place. Answer: C.
Note: the textbook speaks of SEVEN ranks (all options list seven); 'eight' in the stem would include domain, which none of the options contains.
tips: Mnemonic: King Philip Came Over For Good Soup (Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species).

similar_questions.stem: Which rank contains organisms that are MOST similar to each other?
explanation_steps: Similarity increases towards species, the most specific rank. Answer: E.

textbook_ref.section: 2.1 The importance of classification – levels of classification

questions.review_flag: Stem says 'eight levels' but the textbook (and every option) has seven ranks; answer C is unaffected.

questions.stem: What is the scientific name for the horse in the diagram?
questions.image_alt: Branching diagram: a vertical line labelled 'Genus Equus' splits into three branches labelled Species: burchellii (common name Burchell's zebra), caballus (common name horse) and grevyi (common name Grevy's zebra), each with a small drawing of the animal.
explanation_steps: The diagram shows the genus Equus branching into three species: burchellii (Burchell's zebra), caballus (horse) and grevyi (Grevy's zebra).
Binomial nomenclature: scientific name = Genus (capital) + species (small letter), both in italics. Horse = Equus caballus. Answer: A.
'Equus horse' and 'Caballus horse' mix a scientific and a common name.
tips: Genus name first (capitalised), species epithet second (lower case); underline when handwritten.

similar_questions.stem: The scientific name of humans is Homo sapiens. Which part is the genus?
explanation_steps: The first, capitalised word is the genus. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Physical digestion includes all of the following except
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'The taking in and moistening of food with saliva, and chewing by teeth, is called mechanical digestion.' So ingestion (taking in) and lubrication (moistening) are counted; peristalsis also moves and churns food physically.
Hydrolysis is the enzyme-catalysed breakdown of large molecules by water – CHEMICAL digestion. Answer: C.
Assimilation (use of absorbed nutrients by cells) comes after absorption and is not part of digestion at all, so D is also defensible.
tips: Physical/mechanical: chewing, churning, peristalsis, emulsification by bile. Chemical: enzymes (hydrolysis).

similar_questions.stem: Which is an example of chemical digestion?

options.C: Salivary amylase breaking starch into maltose

explanation_steps: Enzymatic breakdown (hydrolysis) is chemical digestion. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Two options are not physical digestion: C (hydrolysis = chemical digestion, keyed) and D (assimilation is not digestion at all – textbook p.22/39). Both accepted. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: The diagram below represents the leaf of
questions.image_alt: Drawing of a broad, heart-shaped leaf with a central midrib and many branching veins forming a net pattern.
explanation_steps: The leaf is broad with a central midrib and branching veins forming a net – reticulate (net) venation.
Net venation is typical of dicotyledons; monocots have parallel veins, gymnosperms needle- or scale-like leaves. Answer: D.
tips: Dicot: net veins, two cotyledons, flower parts in 4s/5s, tap root. Monocot: parallel veins, one cotyledon, parts in 3s, fibrous roots.

similar_questions.stem: A leaf with long parallel veins, like maize, belongs to
explanation_steps: Parallel venation = monocot. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The organ responsible for the different types of receptors, represented in the figure below, is the
questions.image_alt: Four drawings of sensory nerve endings labelled cold (a rounded capsule), hot (branched free endings), touch (a flattened club-shaped ending) and pressure (an onion-like layered corpuscle).
explanation_steps: The figure shows receptors labelled cold, hot, touch and pressure.
These are the sensory receptors of the skin (the sense organ of touch, pressure, temperature and pain). Answer: A.
tips: Skin receptors: touch (Meissner), pressure (Pacinian, onion-like), heat, cold, pain (free nerve endings).

similar_questions.stem: Which sense organ contains rods and cones?
explanation_steps: Rods and cones are photoreceptors of the retina. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Neurons communicate information in
explanation_steps: Along a neuron the message travels as an electrical impulse (action potential).
Across a synapse it is passed on chemically by neurotransmitters. Neurons therefore communicate in both electrical and chemical forms. Answer: D.
tips: Nerve impulse = electrochemical: electrical in the axon, chemical at the synapse.

similar_questions.stem: The chemicals that carry a nerve impulse across a synapse are called
explanation_steps: Neurotransmitters, e.g. acetylcholine. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The following sexual characteristics are associated with puberty in males, except
explanation_steps: Testosterone at male puberty causes increased musculature, a deeper voice, broader chest and shoulders and facial/body hair.
Enlargement of the pelvis is a FEMALE puberty change (textbook: breasts develop, enlargement of the pelvis, maturation of ovaries…). Answer: C.
tips: Female: breasts, wider pelvis, menstruation. Male: voice, muscles, beard, broad shoulders.

similar_questions.stem: Which change occurs in girls at puberty?
explanation_steps: Menstruation begins at female puberty. Answer: C.

questions.stem: In the F₁ generation of a monohybrid cross, the phenotypic ratio would be
explanation_steps: In Mendel's monohybrid crosses, crossing two pure-breeding parents gives an F₁ that is ALL of the dominant type; self-pollinating the F₁ gives an F₂ in the phenotypic ratio 3 : 1 (genotypic 1 : 2 : 1).
The only phenotypic monohybrid ratio offered is 3 : 1 (1 : 2 : 1 is the genotypic ratio). The setter evidently means the offspring of the F₁ (i.e. the F₂). Answer: A.
tips: F₁ = uniform (all dominant); F₂ = 3 : 1 phenotype, 1 : 2 : 1 genotype. Test cross (Tt × tt) = 1 : 1.

similar_questions.stem: Two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt × Tt) are crossed. What fraction of the offspring is expected to be short?
explanation_steps: Tt × Tt → TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1; only tt is short = 1/4. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Strictly, the F₁ of a monohybrid cross between pure lines is all dominant (no ratio); 3 : 1 is the F₂ ratio (textbook p.35). A is keyed as the setter's evident intent.

questions.stem: The characteristic of living organisms that enables them to survive in a particular environment is referred to as
explanation_steps: Adaptation is any inherited feature (structure, function or behaviour) that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment. Answer: E.
tips: Adaptation = fit to the environment; responsiveness = reaction to a stimulus.

similar_questions.stem: The thick fur of an Arctic fox is an example of
explanation_steps: Thick fur helps it survive the cold – an adaptation. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1.1 What is biology? – characteristics of living things

additional_textbook_refs.unit: Unit 4 – Plants, Animals and the Environment

questions.stem: If evolution is the study of how organisms originated, ______ is the study of parasites and parasitism.
explanation_steps: Botany = plants; zoology = animals; ecology = organisms and their environment; cytology = cells.
The study of parasites and parasitism is parasitology, which is not among the options. Answer: E.
tips: -ology words: cytology (cells), histology (tissues), microbiology, parasitology, entomology (insects).

similar_questions.stem: The study of cells is called
explanation_steps: Cyto = cell. Answer: B.

questions.stem: A cellular organelle that is found only in animal cells is
explanation_steps: Mitochondria, Golgi apparatus and ER occur in both plant and animal cells; chloroplasts are found only in plant cells.
The textbook: 'Lysosomes are organelles found only in animal cells.' Answer: D.
(Advanced note: plant cells have lysosome-like vacuoles, but the Grade 9 textbook treats lysosomes and centrioles as animal-only.)
tips: Plant only: cell wall, chloroplast, large central vacuole. Animal only (textbook): centrioles, lysosomes.

similar_questions.stem: Which structure is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
explanation_steps: The cellulose cell wall is plant-only. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The name "Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum" denotes the sharing of which of the following cellular structures on the surface of the endoplasm?
explanation_steps: Rough ER looks rough because its surface is studded with ribosomes, which synthesise proteins; smooth ER lacks ribosomes. Answer: C.
tips: Rough ER = ribosomes → protein; smooth ER → lipids.

similar_questions.stem: The organelle that makes proteins is the
explanation_steps: Ribosomes synthesise proteins. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Carbohydrates are made up of the following atoms except
explanation_steps: Carbohydrates contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, usually with H : O = 2 : 1 (e.g. glucose C₆H₁₂O₆).
Nitrogen is found in proteins and nucleic acids, not in carbohydrates. Answer: B.
tips: CHO = carbohydrates and fats; CHON(S) = proteins; CHONP = nucleic acids.

similar_questions.stem: Which element is present in all proteins but absent from carbohydrates?
explanation_steps: Amino acids contain an amino group (–NH₂). Answer: D.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms

questions.stem: The classification of lipids as saturated or unsaturated fats is according to the number of

options.A: hydrogen atoms present in their fatty acid molecules.
options.C: carbon atoms present in their fatty acid molecules.
options.D: hydrogen atoms in their glycerol molecules.
options.E: oxygen atoms present in their glycerol molecules.

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'According to the number of hydrogen atoms present in their fatty acid molecules, fats are usually classified as saturated or unsaturated fats.'
Saturated fatty acids carry the maximum number of H atoms (no C=C double bonds); unsaturated ones have fewer H atoms (one or more C=C). Answer: A.
tips: Saturated: animal fats, solid at room temperature. Unsaturated: vegetable oils, liquid.

similar_questions.stem: Which is mainly an unsaturated fat?
explanation_steps: Vegetable oils are mostly unsaturated. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Protein substances produced by some group of white blood cells in response to foreign antigens are
explanation_steps: When an antigen enters the body, B-lymphocytes (a group of white blood cells) produce specific proteins called antibodies that bind to and neutralise it. Answer: D.
tips: Antigen = foreign substance that triggers a response; antibody = protein made against it.

similar_questions.stem: Which cells produce antibodies?
explanation_steps: B cells (plasma cells) make antibodies. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The system that is designed to defend our body against microbes and parasites that cause disease is the
explanation_steps: The stem quotes the textbook almost word for word: 'The IMMUNE SYSTEM is designed to defend our body against microbes like bacteria and viruses, toxins and parasites that cause different illnesses and diseases.'
The immune system is not among the options, so the textbook-based answer is E.
However, the lymphatic system (lymph nodes, tonsils, lymphocytes) is a major part of the body's defence, so D is also defensible.
tips: Unit 3 = lymphatic system (transport of lymph, defence); Unit 4 = immune system (defence against pathogens).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is part of the body's first line of defence?
explanation_steps: Physical barriers (skin, mucus) are the first line. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: The stem copies the textbook's definition of the IMMUNE system (G10 p.99), which is not an option, so E is keyed; D (lymphatic system) is also accepted because it is part of body defence. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: Cartilage is gradually converted to bone by a process called
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Cartilage is gradually converted to bone by a process called ossification.' Answer: C.
Calcification (deposition of calcium salts) is only one step of ossification.
tips: Ossification = bone formation (os = bone).

similar_questions.stem: Much of the skeleton of a human foetus is made of
explanation_steps: The foetal skeleton is largely cartilage, later ossified. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The disease called "marasmus" is associated with
explanation_steps: Marasmus is a severe protein–energy malnutrition in young children: extreme wasting of muscle and fat (thin, 'old-man' face).
The textbook treats marasmus (with kwashiorkor) as a protein-deficiency disease. Answer: E.
tips: Kwashiorkor: protein deficiency with oedema (swollen belly). Marasmus: protein and energy deficiency with wasting.

similar_questions.stem: A child with a swollen belly, oedema and reddish hair due to lack of protein has
explanation_steps: Kwashiorkor. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms

questions.stem: Answer questions 19 and 20 using the following figure. The structure represented by the letter "X" is
questions.image_alt: Drawing of a rod-shaped bacterial cell with a layered outer boundary (capsule, cell wall, cell membrane), granular cytoplasm and a coiled nucleoid region; a long whip-like thread trails from one end. Label X with an arrow points to this long thread.
explanation_steps: The figure is a rod-shaped bacterium. X points to the long, whip-like thread trailing from one end of the cell.
This is the flagellum, used for locomotion. Pili are short, hair-like projections; the capsid is the protein coat of a VIRUS. Answer: D.
tips: Flagellum = long whip for movement; pili = short hairs for attachment/conjugation.

similar_questions.stem: The short hair-like structures on the surface of many bacteria that help them attach to surfaces are
explanation_steps: Pili (fimbriae). Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.4.1 The structures and forms of bacteria

questions.stem: Some members of the group, where the above organism belongs, can cause all of the following diseases except
questions.image_alt: Drawing of a rod-shaped bacterial cell with a layered outer boundary (capsule, cell wall, cell membrane), granular cytoplasm and a coiled nucleoid region; a long whip-like thread trails from one end. Label X with an arrow points to this long thread.
explanation_steps: The organism is a bacterium. Gonorrhoea (Neisseria), syphilis (Treponema), tuberculosis (Mycobacterium) and anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) are bacterial diseases.
Rabies is caused by a VIRUS (spread by the bite of infected dogs). Answer: D.
tips: Viral: rabies, HIV/AIDS, polio, measles, influenza, common cold. Bacterial: TB, cholera, typhoid, anthrax, gonorrhoea, syphilis.

similar_questions.stem: Which disease is caused by a virus?
explanation_steps: Measles is viral. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.4.2 Economic importance of bacteria – bacterial diseases

questions.stem: Which of the following group of bacteria are associated with nitrogen fixation?
explanation_steps: Rhizobium lives in the root nodules of leguminous plants (beans, peas) and fixes atmospheric nitrogen into ammonium compounds – a mutualistic relationship.
Mycobacterium causes TB, Salmonella typhoid/food poisoning, Escherichia lives in the gut. Answer: B.
tips: Rhizobium + legume root nodules = nitrogen fixation.

similar_questions.stem: Farmers grow beans before maize because bean root nodules
explanation_steps: Rhizobium enriches the soil with nitrogen compounds. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Lamarck's 'Theory of Organic Evolution' is also referred to

options.D: "the theory of inheritance of acquired characters".

explanation_steps: Lamarck proposed that organs used often become stronger and unused organs weaken (use and disuse), and that such acquired characters are passed on to offspring (inheritance of acquired characters).
His theory is known by both names. B and C are Mendel's laws. Answer: E.
tips: Lamarck: giraffe stretched its neck (use) and passed the longer neck on. Darwin: natural selection.

similar_questions.stem: Which scientist proposed the theory of natural selection?
explanation_steps: Charles Darwin (with Wallace). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct about photosynthesis?

options.A: The light reaction converts light energy into chemical energy.
options.B: The light reaction occurs whether light is present or not.
options.C: The dark reaction of photosynthesis occurs only in the absence of light.
options.D: The dark reaction forms simple sugar using oxygen and hydrogen.

explanation_steps: The textbook: in the light reaction 'light energy is converted into chemical energy'. Answer: A.

B is false (it needs light). C is false: the dark reaction is light-INDEPENDENT – it can occur in light or dark. D is false: the dark reaction makes sugar from CO₂ (and hydrogen from the light reaction); oxygen is a by-product of the light reaction.
tips: Light reaction: light → ATP + NADPH, water split, O₂ released. Dark reaction (Calvin cycle): CO₂ → sugar.

similar_questions.stem: The oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from
explanation_steps: Water is split in the light reaction. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is incorrect about the human heart?

options.B: The right side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs.
options.C: The left side of the heart pumps blood to the remaining tissues of the body.
options.D: The heart is located in the thoracic cavity above the lungs.
options.E: A heart of an adult person has approximately the size of a closed fist.

explanation_steps: The heart is a double pump: the right side sends blood to the lungs (pulmonary circulation), the left side to the rest of the body (systemic circulation). It is about the size of a closed fist.
It lies in the thoracic cavity BETWEEN the two lungs (slightly to the left), not above them. Answer: D.
tips: Heart position: thoracic cavity, between the lungs, behind the sternum, above the diaphragm.

similar_questions.stem: Which chamber pumps oxygenated blood to the body?
explanation_steps: The left ventricle pumps into the aorta. Answer: D.

questions.stem: The following substances are metabolic wastes, in most mammals, except
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'The main metabolic wastes in most mammals are urea, excess water and salts, red pigments and carbon dioxide.'
All four listed substances are metabolic wastes, so none is an exception. Answer: E.
tips: Red (bile) pigments come from the breakdown of haemoglobin in the liver and leave with the faeces and urine.

similar_questions.stem: Which organ excretes most of the urea?
explanation_steps: The kidneys excrete urea in urine (the liver makes it). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following hormones stimulates the production of milk from the mother's mammary glands, following birth?
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Prolactin causes the mammary glands in breasts to develop and produce milk in women who are breastfeeding.'
Oxytocin causes uterine contractions and the ejection (let-down) of milk, not its production; ADH controls water reabsorption; thyroxine and calcitonin are thyroid hormones.
Prolactin is not listed. Answer: E.
tips: Prolactin = milk PRODUCTION; oxytocin = milk EJECTION and labour contractions.

similar_questions.stem: Which hormone causes contraction of the uterus during childbirth?
explanation_steps: Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct about the thyroid gland?

options.A: The thyroid gland is the largest endocrine gland in the body.
options.B: The secretion and size of the gland is controlled by the amount of calcium in the body.
options.C: The thyroid gland is critical to the healthy development and maturation of vertebrates.
options.D: The thyroid gland is located in the lower part of the brain.

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'The thyroid gland is critical to the healthy development and maturation of vertebrates… The thyroid gland is the largest endocrine gland in the body.' – A and C are correct.
Its activity is controlled by TSH from the pituitary and needs iodine (not calcium) – B false; it lies in the neck in front of the trachea, not in the brain – D false. Answer: E.
tips: Thyroid: neck, largest endocrine gland, thyroxine (needs iodine) and calcitonin.

similar_questions.stem: Lack of iodine in the diet causes
explanation_steps: Without iodine thyroxine cannot be made and the thyroid enlarges. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The human axial skeleton encompasses the following bones, except the bones of the
explanation_steps: The axial skeleton forms the central axis: skull, vertebral column and thorax (ribs and sternum).
The limbs (with the pectoral and pelvic girdles) form the appendicular skeleton. Answer: D.
tips: Axial = axis (skull, spine, ribs, sternum). Appendicular = appendages (limbs, girdles).

similar_questions.stem: Which bone belongs to the appendicular skeleton?
explanation_steps: The femur is a limb bone. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The structure called the "loop of Henle" is located in the medulla of the
explanation_steps: The loop of Henle is the U-shaped part of the nephron, the functional unit of the kidney; it dips into the renal medulla and helps reabsorb water and salts. Answer: C.
tips: Nephron: Bowman's capsule (cortex) → proximal tubule → loop of Henle (medulla) → distal tubule → collecting duct.

similar_questions.stem: The functional unit of the kidney is the
explanation_steps: Each kidney has about a million nephrons. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 6.2 The excretory organs – kidney and nephron

questions.stem: In the 'Theory of Natural Selection', the factor that involves competition is
explanation_steps: Darwin: organisms produce more offspring than can survive (over-production); because resources are limited, individuals compete for food, space and mates – the struggle for existence.
Those with favourable variations survive (survival of the fittest) and pass them on. The competition itself is the struggle for existence. Answer: C.
tips: Darwin's steps: over-production → variation → struggle for existence → survival of the fittest → inheritance → new species.

similar_questions.stem: In Darwin's theory, organisms with favourable variations are more likely to survive and reproduce. This is called
explanation_steps: Survival of the fittest (natural selection). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements is correct about mutualism? It is

options.A: a symbiotic relationship in which only one organism benefits.
options.B: an association where both organisms benefit from each other.
options.C: a symbiotic relationship in which one organism benefits without affecting the other one.
options.D: the food relationship between a predator and a prey.

explanation_steps: Mutualism: both partners benefit (e.g. Rhizobium and legumes, lichens).
C describes commensalism; A (one benefits, the other harmed) describes parasitism; D is predation. Answer: B.
tips: Mutualism +/+, commensalism +/0, parasitism +/−.

similar_questions.stem: A tapeworm living in the human intestine is an example of
explanation_steps: The tapeworm benefits and the host is harmed. Answer: C.

questions.stem: A terrestrial biome that is characterized by low rainfall and the presence of shrubs and small trees is
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Grasslands are characterized by a low rainfall and the presence of shrubs and small trees.'
Deserts have VERY low and infrequent rainfall; taiga is a cold coniferous forest; temperate deciduous forests have moderate-to-high rainfall. Answer: E.
tips: Grassland: low rainfall, shrubs, small trees, rich soil. Desert: very low rainfall.

similar_questions.stem: Which biome is an almost treeless plain with frozen subsoil?
explanation_steps: Tundra has permafrost. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Animals depend on bacteria and fungi because bacteria and fungi
explanation_steps: Bacteria and fungi are decomposers: they break down dead organisms and wastes, returning nutrients (N, P, C) to the soil and air for producers, on which animals ultimately depend. Answer: B.
tips: Without decomposers, nutrients would stay locked in dead bodies.

similar_questions.stem: Organisms that break down dead organic matter are called
explanation_steps: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Cnidarians have
explanation_steps: Cnidarians (Hydra, jellyfish, sea anemones, corals) are radially symmetrical, have tentacles with stinging cells (cnidocytes) and a body wall of two tissue layers (ectoderm and endoderm, diploblastic).
They do not have bilateral symmetry. So B, C and D are correct – 'All except A'. Answer: E.
tips: Cnidaria: radial symmetry, two layers, one opening, stinging tentacles. Flatworms onwards: bilateral, three layers.

similar_questions.stem: Which animal is a cnidarian?
explanation_steps: Hydra belongs to phylum Cnidaria. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Xerophytes tolerate water scarcity through
explanation_steps: The textbook lists xerophyte adaptations: thick layer of epidermis, extensive root system, water storage tissues, heavy wax/cuticle, hairs on stomata, sunken stomata, rolling leaves, reduced leaf area.
All four options are included. Answer: E.
tips: Xerophytes (cactus, 'Beles' Opuntia): save water (thick cuticle, few/sunken stomata, small leaves), store water, and find water (deep roots).

similar_questions.stem: Plants that live in water, like the water lily, are called
explanation_steps: Hydrophytes live in water. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Plants, Animals and the Environment
textbook_ref.section: 4.2.2 Adaptations of plants to water – xerophytes

questions.stem: One of the following is not a mechanism of animal's adaptation to low temperature.
explanation_steps: Adaptations to cold (textbook 4.3.1) include insulation (fur, feathers, fat), small body projections (small ears and tails reduce heat loss), shivering (produces heat) and a good appetite (more food to fuel heat production), as well as hibernation.
Nocturnal behaviour – being active at night and resting by day – is listed under adaptations to HIGH temperatures (4.3.2, e.g. desert animals, bats). Answer: E.
tips: Cold: conserve and produce heat. Hot: avoid heat (nocturnal, burrowing, aestivation, large ears).

similar_questions.stem: The large ears of a desert fox help it to
explanation_steps: Large surface area radiates heat. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Plants, Animals and the Environment
textbook_ref.section: 4.3.1–4.3.2 Adaptations of animals to low and high temperatures

questions.stem: During the process of absorption, nutrients move from
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'The transfer of these smaller molecules into the bloodstream is termed absorption.' Digested food passes through the villi of the small intestine into the blood capillaries (and fats into lacteals). Answer: C.
Movement from the blood into cells and their use is assimilation.
tips: Digestion → absorption (gut → blood) → assimilation (blood → cells, used) → egestion.

similar_questions.stem: Most absorption of digested food takes place in the
explanation_steps: The small intestine with its villi. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Muscle weakness and cramps can be due to lack of
explanation_steps: The textbook's mineral table: magnesium deficiency → 'muscle weakness (fatigue), cramps'; iron → anaemia; iodine → goitre; calcium → stunted growth, rickets; chlorine → not known. Answer: D.
In medicine, low blood calcium also causes muscle cramps (tetany), so B is also defensible.
tips: Textbook table: Ca – bones, teeth, clotting; Mg – muscle weakness, cramps; Fe – anaemia; I – goitre.

similar_questions.stem: Lack of iron in the diet causes
explanation_steps: Iron is needed for haemoglobin. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: D (magnesium) matches the textbook table (G10 p.13); calcium deficiency (hypocalcaemia) also causes muscle cramps, so B is accepted. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: Alveoli in the lungs are connected to the bronchi by a network of tiny tubes called
explanation_steps: Air passes trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. The bronchioles are the fine branches of the bronchi that end in the alveoli.
Arterioles, venules and capillaries are blood vessels. Answer: D.
tips: Airway order: nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

similar_questions.stem: Gas exchange in the lungs takes place in the
explanation_steps: Thin-walled alveoli surrounded by capillaries. Answer: D.

textbook_ref.section: 5.1 The respiratory tract – bronchi and bronchioles

questions.stem: Air in the alveoli following inhalation has the highest concentration of one of the following gases.
explanation_steps: Freshly inhaled air brings oxygen (≈ 21 % in atmospheric air, ≈ 14 % in alveolar air); CO₂ in alveolar air is only ≈ 5 %; hydrogen and CO are practically absent.
Of the gases listed, oxygen has the highest concentration. Answer: D. (Nitrogen, ≈ 78 %, is the most abundant gas overall but is not an option.)
tips: Inhaled air: O₂ 21 %, CO₂ 0.04 %. Exhaled air: O₂ 16 %, CO₂ 4 %.

similar_questions.stem: Compared with inhaled air, exhaled air contains
explanation_steps: CO₂ from respiration is added. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Part of the ear most responsible for transmitting impulses to the brain is the
explanation_steps: The pinna and auditory canal collect sound; the ear drum and ossicles transmit vibrations mechanically.
The cochlea (inner ear) contains the hair-cell receptors that convert vibrations into nerve impulses, which the auditory nerve carries to the brain. Answer: B.
tips: Sound path: pinna → canal → ear drum → ossicles → oval window → cochlea → auditory nerve → brain.

similar_questions.stem: The part of the ear responsible for balance is the
explanation_steps: Semicircular canals detect head movement. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The mitochondria of the sperm cell are found at the
explanation_steps: A sperm has a head (nucleus and acrosome with enzymes), a middle piece packed with mitochondria that release energy for swimming, and a tail (flagellum). Answer: C.
tips: Head = genes + acrosome; middle piece = mitochondria (energy); tail = movement.

similar_questions.stem: The acrosome of a sperm contains

options.B: enzymes that help penetrate the egg

explanation_steps: Acrosomal enzymes digest the egg's coat. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2 Male reproductive system – structure of the sperm

questions.stem: Smooth muscle is found in all of the following structures except the
explanation_steps: Smooth (involuntary) muscle lines the airways, the digestive tract, blood vessels and the skin (arrector pili muscles).
The heart wall is made of CARDIAC muscle. Answer: D.
tips: Three muscle types: skeletal (voluntary), smooth (internal organs), cardiac (heart only).

similar_questions.stem: Which type of muscle never tires and is found only in the heart?
explanation_steps: Cardiac muscle. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is incorrect about skeletal muscles?

options.D: They have an origin and insertion end.

explanation_steps: Skeletal muscles work in antagonistic pairs (flexor/extensor, e.g. biceps/triceps), each with an origin (fixed end) and insertion (moving end), and move bones to lift things.
Peristalsis – the wave-like contraction that moves food along the gut – is done by SMOOTH muscle. Answer: B.
tips: Biceps (flexor) bends the elbow; triceps (extensor) straightens it.

similar_questions.stem: When the biceps contracts, the triceps
explanation_steps: Antagonistic muscles: one contracts while the other relaxes. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The part of a seed embryo that emerges first during germination is the
explanation_steps: After the seed absorbs water, the radicle (embryonic root) bursts through the seed coat first, anchoring the seedling and absorbing water; then the plumule (embryonic shoot) grows up.
Epigeal and hypogeal are types of germination, not parts. Answer: A.
tips: Radicle → root (first); plumule → shoot.

similar_questions.stem: In epigeal germination (bean), the cotyledons
explanation_steps: The hypocotyl elongates and lifts the cotyledons above ground. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Plant hormones

options.A: interact with specific target tissues of the plant.
options.C: affect plant's ability to respond to the environment.
options.D: can stimulate or inhibit plant growth.

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Plant hormones are chemical substances that affect a plant's ability to respond to its environment… they can stimulate or inhibit plant growth. They interact with specific target tissues.'
All statements are correct. Answer: E.
tips: Auxins (cell elongation, tropisms), gibberellins (stem growth, germination), cytokinins (cell division), abscisic acid (dormancy), ethylene (ripening).

similar_questions.stem: Which plant hormone speeds up fruit ripening?
explanation_steps: Ethylene gas. Answer: C.

questions.stem: A plant tissue that is considered as complex tissue is
explanation_steps: Simple permanent tissues consist of one cell type: parenchyma (and its green form chlorenchyma), collenchyma, sclerenchyma.
Complex tissues contain several cell types: xylem (vessels, tracheids, fibres, parenchyma) and phloem (sieve tubes, companion cells, fibres, parenchyma). Answer: D.
tips: Complex = xylem and phloem (vascular tissues).

similar_questions.stem: Which tissue transports water and minerals from roots to leaves?
explanation_steps: Xylem. Answer: B.

questions.stem:
What would be transcribed from this DNA base sequence?
3′-C-C-G-A-A-T-G-T-C-5′
explanation_steps: Transcription makes mRNA complementary to the DNA template: C→G, G→C, A→U, T→A (RNA has uracil, not thymine).
Template 3′-CCGAATGTC-5′ → mRNA bases GGCUUACAG.
The strands are antiparallel, so the mRNA runs 5′→3′ opposite the template: 5′-GGCUUACAG-3′. Answer: C.
B and D contain T (DNA, not RNA); A has the wrong direction; E has a T.
tips: mRNA: complementary, antiparallel, U instead of T.

similar_questions.stem: Transcribe the DNA template 3′-TACGGA-5′.
explanation_steps: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C, antiparallel: 5′-AUGCCU-3′. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Significance of meiosis is associated with
explanation_steps: Meiosis halves the chromosome number (2n → n) to form gametes and creates genetic variation (crossing over, independent assortment); fertilisation restores 2n. It is therefore essential for sexual reproduction.
Growth, repair (maintenance) and asexual reproduction depend on mitosis. Answer: A.
tips: Mitosis: growth, repair, asexual reproduction (2n → 2n). Meiosis: gametes (2n → n).

similar_questions.stem: A human cell with 46 chromosomes undergoes meiosis. Each gamete has
explanation_steps: Meiosis halves the number: 23. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Hemophilia is a sex-linked disease with a recessive trait in humans. If a father and a son are both hemophiliacs, but the mother is normal, her genotype must be
explanation_steps: A son receives his X chromosome from his MOTHER (and Y from his father). A haemophiliac son (XʰY) therefore got Xʰ from his mother.
The mother is phenotypically normal, so she also carries a normal Xᴴ: she is a carrier, XᴴXʰ. Answer: B.
XʰXʰ would make her haemophiliac; XᴴXᴴ could not give Xʰ; XʰY and XᴴY are male genotypes.
tips: Sons inherit X-linked traits from their mothers.

similar_questions.stem: A carrier woman (XᴴXʰ) marries a normal man (XᴴY). What proportion of their SONS is expected to be haemophiliac?
explanation_steps: Sons get Xᴴ or Xʰ from the mother with equal chance → 1/2. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct about the pericardial fluid?

options.A: It is found between the pericardium and the heart.
options.B: It is found between the heart and the thoracic cavity.
options.C: It reduces friction between the pericardium and the heart.
options.D: It reduces friction between the heart and the lungs.

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'The pericardial fluid present between the pericardium and the heart itself reduces friction between them.'
Both A and C are correct. Answer: E.
tips: Pericardium = double membrane around the heart; the fluid in between is a lubricant.

similar_questions.stem: The membrane that surrounds the lungs is the
explanation_steps: The pleural membranes and pleural fluid. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The release of male sex hormones (androgen) into the bloodstream is stimulated by
explanation_steps: The textbook: the interstitial cells of the testes, 'when stimulated by the luteinizing hormone, … release androgens (e.g. testosterone) into the bloodstream.'
FSH stimulates sperm production; aldosterone and cortisol are adrenal hormones. Answer: B.
tips: In males: LH (ICSH) → testosterone; FSH → sperm formation.

similar_questions.stem: In females, the hormone that triggers ovulation is
explanation_steps: The LH surge causes ovulation. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Hypoglycemia is a health problem associated with

options.A: high level of sugar in the blood.
options.B: high level of protein in the blood.
options.C: low level of sugar in the blood.
options.D: lack of iodine in the body.

explanation_steps: Hypo = low, glyc = sugar, -aemia = blood: hypoglycaemia is an abnormally low blood-glucose level (e.g. after too much insulin), causing dizziness, sweating and even coma. Answer: C.
High blood sugar is hyperglycaemia (diabetes mellitus).
tips: Insulin lowers blood sugar; glucagon raises it.

similar_questions.stem: Diabetes mellitus is characterised by
explanation_steps: Hyperglycaemia due to lack of insulin action. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 5.1.1 The need for homeostasis – blood sugar

questions.stem: In a particular place, a cricket is active at night and a grasshopper is active during the day time. These animals are said to have different
explanation_steps: They share the same place (habitat, ecosystem, environment), but differ in their role and way of life – including the time when they are active and feed.
An organism's role or 'profession', including when and how it feeds, is its ecological niche. Answer: A.
tips: Habitat = address (where); niche = profession (what it does, when, how).

similar_questions.stem: Two species cannot occupy exactly the same niche in the same habitat for long because of
explanation_steps: Competitive exclusion. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.1 What is ecology? – habitat and niche

questions.stem: Which of the following statements describes best the pyramid of biomass?

options.A: It compares the amount of biomass of an organism at each trophic level.
options.B: It is based on the amount of energy produced per unit area by different trophic levels over a given time period.
options.C: The shape of the pyramid narrows sharply from producers at the base to carnivores at the apex.
options.D: It compares the number of individuals at each trophic level.

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'The pyramid of biomass compares the amount of biomass of an organism at each trophic level. The shape of the pyramid narrows sharply from producers at the base to carnivores at the apex.'
B describes the pyramid of energy; D the pyramid of numbers. Answer: E.
tips: Pyramids: numbers (individuals), biomass (dry mass per area), energy (energy per area per time – always upright).

similar_questions.stem: Which ecological pyramid is always upright?
explanation_steps: Energy always decreases up the levels. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The pancreas, liver, and gallbladder help digestion in these ways, respectively

options.A: making enzymes; making bile; and storing bile.
options.B: producing saliva; digesting carbohydrates; and eliminating waste.
options.C: producing bile; producing enzymes; and eliminating waste.
options.D: making acids; producing digestive juices; and storing enzymes.
options.E: making bile, producing saliva, eliminating waste.

explanation_steps: Pancreas → pancreatic juice with enzymes (amylase, trypsin, lipase).
Liver → makes bile, which emulsifies fats.
Gall bladder → stores and concentrates bile, releasing it into the duodenum. Answer: A.
tips: Liver MAKES bile; gall bladder STORES it; bile has no enzymes.

similar_questions.stem: Bile helps digestion by
explanation_steps: Bile salts break fat into droplets. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.3 Accessory organs – liver, gall bladder and pancreas

questions.stem: Which lymphoid tissues trap and remove bacteria entering the throat?
explanation_steps: The tonsils are masses of lymphoid tissue at the back of the throat; they trap and destroy bacteria and viruses entering through the mouth and nose. Answer: A.
The thymus matures T-cells; the spleen filters blood; axillary (armpit) and inguinal (groin) nodes filter lymph from the limbs.
tips: Tonsillitis = inflamed tonsils.

similar_questions.stem: The lymphoid organ that filters blood and destroys old red blood cells is the
explanation_steps: The spleen. Answer: C.

questions.stem: When we smell irritating odor, we sneeze; the part of the brain responsible for this phenomenon is the
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'Other reflexes controlled by centres in the medulla include coughing, swallowing and sneezing.' Answer: A.
The cerebrum controls voluntary actions and thinking, the cerebellum balance and coordination, the hypothalamus temperature and hunger.
tips: Medulla: breathing, heartbeat, blood pressure, coughing, sneezing, swallowing, vomiting.

similar_questions.stem: The part of the brain that coordinates balance and posture is the
explanation_steps: The cerebellum. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 8.2 Parts of the human nervous system – medulla oblongata

questions.stem: An egg cell can never be fertilized during one of the following phases of the menstrual cycle.
explanation_steps: Ovulation occurs around day 14, at the end of the proliferative (follicular) phase; the ovum survives about a day, early in the luteal (secretory) phase.
During the menstrual phase (days 1–5) the endometrium is being shed and no mature ovum is available, so fertilisation cannot occur. Answer: A.
tips: Menstrual (1–5) → proliferative/follicular (6–14, ovulation) → secretory/luteal (15–28).

similar_questions.stem: Ovulation normally occurs around day ___ of a 28-day cycle.
explanation_steps: About day 14. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not necessary for protein synthesis in the cytoplasm?
explanation_steps: Translation in the cytoplasm needs mRNA (the message), tRNA (brings amino acids), ribosomes made of rRNA and protein, amino acids, enzymes and ATP.
DNA stays in the nucleus; it is needed for transcription, but not directly in the cytoplasm. Answer: D.
tips: Transcription (nucleus): DNA → mRNA. Translation (cytoplasm, ribosome): mRNA → protein.

similar_questions.stem: The molecule that carries amino acids to the ribosome is
explanation_steps: Transfer RNA with its anticodon. Answer: B.

questions.stem:
Match the biological terms in column A with the appropriate description in column B. (2.5 points)
1.1 Plants   1.2 Fungi   1.3 Bacteria   1.4 Animalia   1.5 Protista
A. Prokaryotes found in soil, water, and humans
B. Mostly single-celled or simple multi-cellular organisms
C. Eukaryotic organisms that use extracellular digestion
D. Multi-cellular organisms that lack cell wall, heterotrophs
E. Multi-cellular organisms that have cell walls, photosynthetic

stem_tables.title: Question 1
rows: A. Prokaryotes found in soil, water, and humans
B. Mostly single-celled or simple multi-cellular organisms
C. Eukaryotic organisms that use extracellular digestion
D. Multi-cellular organisms that lack cell wall, heterotrophs
E. Multi-cellular organisms that have cell walls, photosynthetic

explanation_steps: Plants: multicellular, cellulose cell walls, photosynthetic → E.
Fungi: eukaryotes that secrete enzymes onto their food and absorb the products (extracellular digestion) → C.
Bacteria (Monera): prokaryotes living in soil, water and on/in humans → A.
Animalia: multicellular heterotrophs without cell walls → D.
Protista: mostly single-celled or simple multicellular eukaryotes → B.
marking_points: ½ point for each correct match (5 × ½ = 2.5)
tips: Kingdoms by cell type: Monera prokaryotic; all others eukaryotic. Nutrition: plants autotrophic; fungi absorb; animals ingest.

similar_questions.stem: To which kingdom does each belong: (a) yeast, (b) Amoeba, (c) Escherichia coli, (d) moss?
explanation_steps: Yeast is a unicellular fungus; Amoeba a protozoan; E. coli a bacterium; mosses are bryophytes (plants).

questions.stem: What are the two raw materials required for aerobic respiration? (1 point)
explanation_steps: Aerobic respiration: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (ATP).
The raw materials (reactants) are glucose and oxygen; CO₂ and water are the products.
marking_points: ½ point each: glucose (accept sugar/food), oxygen
tips: Respiration is roughly the reverse of photosynthesis.

similar_questions.stem: Name the two products of aerobic respiration apart from energy.
explanation_steps: From the respiration equation.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms

questions.stem: In the life cycle of plants, the 3.1 ______ generation alternates with the 3.2 ______ generation. (1 point)
questions.answer: 3.1 sporophyte (diploid, spore-producing); 3.2 gametophyte (haploid, gamete-producing) – either order.
explanation_steps: Plants show alternation of generations: a diploid (2n) sporophyte produces spores by meiosis; spores grow into a haploid (n) gametophyte, which produces gametes; fertilisation gives a new sporophyte.
marking_points: ½ point each for sporophyte and gametophyte (either order)
tips: Moss: gametophyte dominant. Fern and flowering plants: sporophyte dominant.

similar_questions.stem: Which generation is dominant in a fern?
explanation_steps: The gametophyte is a small prothallus.

questions.stem: ______ is part of a microscope that brings an image into focus and magnifies it. (0.5 points)
explanation_steps: The textbook's table of microscope parts: 'Objective lens – brings image into focus and magnifies it'; ocular lens (eyepiece) – magnifies the image; coarse/fine adjustment knobs – bring the image into focus.
marking_points: Objective lens (0.5); do not accept eyepiece or adjustment knob
tips: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective.

similar_questions.stem: A microscope has a 10× eyepiece and a 40× objective. What is the total magnification?

questions.stem: The lining of the small intestine contains specialized lymphatic capillaries called ______. (0.5 points)
explanation_steps: Each villus of the small intestine contains blood capillaries and a central lymphatic capillary, the lacteal, which absorbs digested fats (fatty acids and glycerol, as chylomicrons) forming milky chyle.
tips: Villus: capillaries absorb sugars and amino acids; lacteal absorbs fats.

similar_questions.stem: Digested fats are absorbed into the ______ of the villi, whereas glucose enters the ______.
explanation_steps: Fats go to lymph, sugars to blood.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2.6 The small intestine – villi and lacteals

questions.stem: Label the different parts of the following human female reproductive system. (2 points)
questions.image_alt: Front view of the human female reproductive system: a central pear-shaped uterus shown partly in section, with a tube curving out on each side to a fringed end beside an oval ovary; below, the narrow cervix opens into the vagina. Label 6.1 points to the oval ovary on the right, 6.2 to the cervix at the lower end of the uterus, 6.3 to the wall/cavity of the uterus on the left, and 6.4 to the tube on the upper left.

subparts.question: Label 6.1
steps: Oval organ beside the fringed end of the tube.

explanation_steps: 6.1 points to the oval body at the end of the right-hand tube – the ovary, which produces ova and female hormones.
6.2 points to the narrow neck at the lower end of the uterus, where it opens into the vagina – the cervix.
6.3 points to the thick-walled, pear-shaped central organ – the uterus, where the embryo implants and develops.
6.4 points to the tube running from the ovary region to the uterus – the oviduct (Fallopian tube), where fertilisation occurs.
marking_points: ½ point for each correct label
tips: Path of the ovum: ovary → oviduct (fertilisation) → uterus (implantation).

similar_questions.stem: In which part of the female reproductive system does fertilisation normally take place?
explanation_steps: The ovum meets sperm in the upper third of the oviduct.

questions.stem: The single bone of the human upper arm is called 7.1 ______, whereas the upper bone of the leg is called 7.2 ______. (1 point)
explanation_steps: Upper arm: humerus; forearm: radius and ulna.
Thigh (upper leg): femur – the longest and strongest bone; lower leg: tibia and fibula.
tips: Arm: humerus / radius + ulna. Leg: femur / tibia + fibula.

similar_questions.stem: Name the two bones of the forearm.
explanation_steps: The radius is on the thumb side.

questions.stem:
The following table represents the summary of blood compatibilities in blood transfusion. Complete the information by filling the right blood type. (4 points)
Blood type | Can receive from | Can give to
A | 8.1 | 8.2
B | 8.3 | 8.4
AB | 8.5 | 8.6
O | 8.7 | 8.8
explanation_steps: A recipient must not receive red cells carrying an antigen that his plasma has antibodies against.
Group A (antigen A, anti-B): receives A and O; gives to A and AB.
Group B (antigen B, anti-A): receives B and O; gives to B and AB.
Group AB (both antigens, no antibodies): receives from all – universal recipient; gives only to AB.
Group O (no antigens, anti-A and anti-B): receives only O; gives to all – universal donor.
marking_points: ½ point for each fully correct box (8 × ½ = 4)
tips: O = universal donor; AB = universal recipient.

similar_questions.stem: A patient with blood group B needs a transfusion. Which two blood groups can safely be given?
explanation_steps: Neither carries the A antigen.

questions.stem: Name the organs that are found in the shoot system of an angiosperm plant. (2 points)
questions.answer: Stem, leaves, buds, flowers and fruits (with seeds).
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'A plant has two organ systems: the shoot system and the root system. The shoot system is above ground and includes the organs such as leaves, buds, stems, flowers and fruits.'
marking_points: ½ point each for any four of: stem, leaves, buds, flowers, fruits (seeds) – maximum 2
tips: Shoot = above ground; root system = below ground (roots).

similar_questions.stem: Name the organ system of a plant found below the ground and give two functions.
similar_questions.answer: Root system – anchorage and absorption of water and minerals (also storage).
explanation_steps: Roots anchor and absorb.

questions.stem: What is the function of chlorophyll? (0.5 points)
questions.answer: Chlorophyll absorbs (traps) light energy from the sun for photosynthesis.
explanation_steps: Chlorophyll, the green pigment in chloroplasts, absorbs mainly red and blue light; this energy drives the light reaction (splitting water and making ATP), which is converted into chemical energy in sugar.
tips: Chlorophyll reflects green light – that is why leaves look green.

similar_questions.stem: In which organelle is chlorophyll found?
explanation_steps: Chloroplasts are the site of photosynthesis.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Metabolic Processes and Energy Transfers in Living Organisms

questions.stem:
Define the following terms. (4 points)
11.1 Ecology
11.2 Ribosome
11.3 Cardiac muscle
11.4 Genotype
questions.answer: 11.1 Ecology: the study of the relationships of organisms with one another and with their (physical) environment. 11.2 Ribosome: a tiny organelle (made of rRNA and protein), free or on rough ER, that is the site of protein synthesis. 11.3 Cardiac muscle: the involuntary, striated, branched muscle found only in the wall of the heart, which contracts rhythmically without tiring. 11.4 Genotype: the genetic make-up (set of alleles) of an organism for a trait, e.g. TT, Tt or tt.

subparts.question: Ecology
subparts.answer: The study of the interactions of organisms with each other and with their environment.

subparts.question: Ribosome
subparts.answer: A small organelle made of RNA and protein that is the site of protein synthesis.
steps: Free or attached to rough ER.

subparts.question: Cardiac muscle
subparts.answer: Involuntary, striated, branched muscle found only in the heart wall.

subparts.question: Genotype
subparts.answer: The genetic constitution (combination of alleles) of an organism, e.g. Tt.

explanation_steps: Give a precise one-sentence definition of each term using textbook wording.
marking_points: 1 point for each correct definition (½ for a partially correct one)
tips: Genotype = genes (alleles); phenotype = observable character.

similar_questions.stem: Define phenotype and give an example.
similar_questions.answer: The observable characteristics of an organism resulting from its genotype and environment, e.g. tall or short pea plant.
explanation_steps: Phenotype is what you see.

questions.stem: Mention any two adaptation mechanisms of living organisms to environmental stress factors. (1 point)
questions.answer: Any two, e.g. hibernation (winter sleep in cold), aestivation (summer dormancy in heat/drought), migration, nocturnal behaviour, insulation (fur, fat, feathers), shivering, sweating/panting, water-storage tissues and thick cuticle in xerophytes, deep root systems, leaf fall in dry season, burrowing.
explanation_steps: Environmental stresses include extreme temperatures, drought, salinity and low oxygen.

Organisms respond with structural adaptations (fur, thick cuticle, water-storage tissue), physiological adaptations (shivering, sweating, concentrated urine) and behavioural adaptations (hibernation, aestivation, migration, nocturnal activity).
marking_points: ½ point each for any two valid adaptations
tips: Name the mechanism and the stress it answers (e.g. aestivation – heat and drought).

similar_questions.stem: Distinguish between hibernation and aestivation.
similar_questions.answer: Hibernation is a dormant state during cold winters; aestivation is a dormant state during hot, dry periods.
explanation_steps: Both reduce metabolism to survive stress.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Plants, Animals and the Environment

questions.stem:
Write the function of the following major veins. (2 points)
13.1 Superior vena cava
13.2 Inferior vena cava
questions.answer: 13.1 Superior vena cava: returns deoxygenated blood from the head, neck and arms (upper body) to the right atrium. 13.2 Inferior vena cava: returns deoxygenated blood from the lower parts of the body (trunk, abdominal organs and legs) to the right atrium.

subparts.question: Superior vena cava
subparts.answer: Brings deoxygenated blood from the head, neck and upper body to the right atrium.

subparts.question: Inferior vena cava
subparts.answer: Brings deoxygenated blood from the lower body to the right atrium.

explanation_steps: The textbook: 'the superior vena cava, which drains blood from regions of the head and neck; and the inferior vena cava, which drains blood from the lower regions of the body' – both empty into the right atrium.
marking_points: 1 point each: correct body region AND return to the heart/right atrium (½ if only one part)
tips: Superior = above the heart; inferior = below the heart; both carry deoxygenated blood.

similar_questions.stem: Which blood vessel carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart?
similar_questions.answer: The pulmonary vein(s), into the left atrium.
explanation_steps: The only veins carrying oxygenated blood.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2 Blood circulation – veins entering the right atrium
